title: Fixing decades of poor defence housing: buy-back, repair plans and lessons
label: 10 September 2026 · Armed forces housing and Annington Homes
summary: The Committee questioned senior Ministry of Defence officials about the 1996 sale of military family homes, the MOD’s 2019–24 work to re-negotiate and repurchase much of the estate from Annington Homes, and the plans to repair and run the homes through a new Defence Housing Service backed by a £9.2bn 10-year fund. Witnesses defended the buy-back as good value, described a decade-long repair and reshaping programme, accepted the 1996 deal was poor, and set out steps to build the skills, governance and partnerships needed — while the Committee pushed for faster progress, clearer short-term spending figures, and stronger safeguards before future asset sales.

Homes the MOD provides for armed forces personnel and their families.

chapters.title: Overview and the buy-back
chapters.takeaway: Officials say the 1996 sale was a mistake, but the 2019–24 work to reclaim homes was a strong, value-for-money outcome.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Today we’re examining the 1996 sale of about 55,000 military homes to Annington and the MOD’s recent buy-back of 36,000 homes for £6bn.

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: The 1996 deal was not one we would do today. The repurchase we completed by 2024 is, by contrast, a good deal and a real success for the Department.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: How did the original contract become so bad that it left taxpayers with big losses and service families in poor homes?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: It was a sale-and-leaseback shaped by the priorities of the time. The public‑sector advisory and appraisal systems we have now didn’t exist then, and incentives in that deal were wrong.

turns.speaker: Chris Kane
turns.text: We need to be confident those mistakes won’t recur. Have you learned the specific lessons from the 1996 deal?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: Yes: understand asset value, model uncertainty, check hidden assumptions and involve external experts early. We’ve changed how we assess large transactions.

chapters.title: Why it took so long to fix the deal
chapters.takeaway: Officials say legal cases, rent renegotiation and new accounting rules were needed to create the leverage to buy back the homes.

turns.speaker: Chris Kane
turns.text: Why did it take from 1996 until about 2019 to make serious progress?

turns.speaker: Mike Green
turns.text: You need two sides to negotiate. Before 2019 we lacked commercial leverage. Court wins on enfranchisement, a rent renegotiation and IFRS 16 changed the position and let Annington come to the table.

turns.speaker: David Brewer
turns.text: The contract’s drafting made potential losses grow fast over time. The steps from 2019 created the conditions where a buy-back was deliverable and saved taxpayers money versus earlier options.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: Was the MOD aware earlier that the deal was damaging?

turns.speaker: Mike Green
turns.text: NAO reports flagged problems earlier, but the combination of legal, accounting and negotiation changes was needed before a realistic buy-back was possible.

chapters.title: Current condition of the homes and repair plans
chapters.takeaway: The estate needs major work: widespread old construction, high reactive repairs, and many homes below modern energy standards; a 10-year improvement programme is planned.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: The Report shows poor maintenance and satisfaction. How are you fixing the negligent approach to upkeep?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: It’s a priority. We created the Defence Housing Service to improve standards and are already seeing satisfaction rise and complaints fall sharply.

turns.speaker: Mike Green
turns.text: When I joined in 2022 we had serious issues like damp and mould. We've fixed the worst cases and compliance problems, but the stock was under‑insulated and under‑maintained for decades.

turns.speaker: David Brewer
turns.text: Most houses were built mid‑20th century and over half are below an EPC D rating. We do about 250,000 reactive repairs a year—disruption to families—and need long‑term work.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: You plan a 10‑year programme. When will families see better homes?

turns.speaker: David Brewer
turns.text: Improvements will be progressive. We’ll double the current run rate of substantial refurbishments and lift standards for the 10–15,000 moves we do each year, but full estate renewal is a multi‑year task.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Ten years seems too slow if recruitment and retention rely on decent housing. Can you move faster?

turns.speaker: Mike Green
turns.text: We prioritise the worst properties first and are improving services now. But fixing decades of neglect properly needs time, money and industry capacity.

chapters.title: Money, timing and transparency
chapters.takeaway: The MOD has a £9.2bn, 10‑year refurbishment commitment; officials defended reprofiling into later years and promised clearer short‑term spending figures.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Aneen, is the £9.2bn conditional on the buy-back? How much will be spent in this Parliament?

turns.speaker: Aneen Blackmore
turns.text: £9.2bn is the 10‑year commitment protected through the DIP. We had to reprofile about £0.8bn out of the current parliamentary period. Over the next four years we plan £2.7bn for service family accommodation.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You must provide precise figures for this financial year across all defence housing lines.

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: You asked recently; we will write with a full breakdown and the figures you requested, including single living accommodation and SFA.

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: Separately, part of the plan is to free up land and build homes for the wider market — up to 100,000 over time — but that is distinct from the SFA programme.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Will any of those homes be used for asylum accommodation or similar pressures?

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: No — the intention is to deliver homes for military use or for the open market, not as part of asylum housing policy.

chapters.title: Governance, skills and market approach
chapters.takeaway: The MOD will set up the Defence Housing Service as an arm’s‑length body, build commercial and development skills, rely on partnerships with private builders, and keep UKGI support.

turns.speaker: Blake Stephenson
turns.text: Do you currently have the skills to run development, regeneration and housing services?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: We are building that capacity through the Defence Housing Service: appointing a chair, recruiting non‑execs and hiring commercial, construction and housing experts now.

turns.speaker: Mike Green
turns.text: DIO has strong operational housing experience—we’re one of the UK’s largest housing providers—but we need to add development skills for major regeneration work.

turns.speaker: Blake Stephenson
turns.text: How will the new body be funded and allowed to use sales receipts or borrowing?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: The Defence Housing Service will be an NDPB. Receipts from sales are available to MOD under the overall agreement; the legislation allows borrowing in principle, but there are no plans for it to borrow to fund core military housing without Treasury agreement.

turns.speaker: Chris Kane
turns.text: Will you compete with private developers or partner with them?

turns.speaker: David Brewer
turns.text: We don’t intend to compete. Our approach is partnership: joint ventures, use of section 106, and leveraging builders’ buying power for refurbishment materials.

turns.speaker: Blake Stephenson
turns.text: Did UK Government Investments (UKGI) help?

turns.speaker: Mike Green
turns.text: Yes—UKGI were essential. They gave detailed financial advice and confidence on the negotiating band. We integrated advisers into a single team rather than outsourcing everything.

chapters.title: Lessons and final points
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses accept the 1996 deal was a strategic error; they argue the buy-back and the Defence Housing Service offer a chance to fix housing if ministers back funding, publish clearer short‑term plans, and sustain oversight.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: The NAO says taxpayers were about £14.5bn worse off by 2024 because of the 1996 sale. How do we avoid repeating that kind of mistake?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Pocklington
turns.text: Avoid deals that prioritise short-term returns over long-term stewardship, model uncertainty properly, align incentives, and bring in expert scrutiny early.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We welcome the buy-back, but press you to speed up improvements, publish specific spending this year, and ensure the new service delivers for families quickly.

turns.speaker: David Brewer
turns.text: We will publish the Defence Housing Service plan in year one of operation, set priorities to attack the worst homes first, and be more transparent about performance.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. We will produce a Report with recommendations; please respond to our follow‑up requests promptly.
